Issued at 233 AM EDT Thu Sep 3 2026

Today-Tonight...Heavy rainfall for East Central Florida has been 
more miss than hit that last few days, but that is likely to start
changing today. Another weak inverted trough has developed over 
the nearby Atlantic waters, and overnight onshore moving showers 
and lightning storms have already been more plentiful, and are 
likely to continue through the morning. Between a weakening 
pressure gradient on the western periphery of the Bermuda high and
troughs in and near the local Atlantic waters, low-level flow 
becomes more southeasterly today, allowing a better defined east 
coast sea breeze (more effective trigger for convection) to 
develop, while also shifting portions of the collision and highest
afternoon storms chances into our area. The weak surface troughs 
and the southeasterly flow they are producing keep moisture well 
above normal (PWATs 2.2-2.4" approaching or exceeding daily 
maximums). Model and upper air soundings continue to show a very 
saturated environment with long-skinny instability profiles (CAPE 
generally 1,000-2,000 J/kg, though some surface based parcels 
could push towards 3,000 J/kg) and warm mid-levels (T500 -5C to 
-4C) characteristic of heavy rainfall/efficient rain makers. In 
addition to more surface triggers that could generate higher 
coverage of convection on our side of the peninsula, weak offshore
steering flow becomes light/variable and storm motion is likely 
to become slow/erratic. Storms and heavy showers will be capable 
of delivering a quick 2-3" of rainfall leading to ponding of water
on roads and minor flooding of urban, low-lying, or poor drainage
areas. HREF guidance indicates there is a very low (up to 5%) 
chance for a few locations to receive locally high amounts +5" 
leading to greater flooding impacts, and the Weather Prediction 
Center has outlooked all of East Central Florida in a Marginal 
(level 1 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall. In addition to the 
rainfall, stronger storms and heavy showers will be capable of 
gusty winds to around 40 mph from water loading. Occasional to 
frequent cloud to ground lightning will accompany thunderstorms.

As for the rest of the forecast, lots of cloud cover keeps 
temperatures seasonable with highs in the U80s-L90s, and lows in 
the muggy 70s. Peak afternoon heat indices 99-106. There is 
Moderate risk of rip currents at the beaches. Always swim near a 
lifeguard and never swim alone.

Friday-Saturday...The parent trough of a low pressure system 
pushing offshore New England and the Canadian Maritimes will dig 
down the eastern seaboard, shoving the ridge over the Southeast 
back to the Central US, and the Bermuda high south. As the surface
ridge axis slides through Florida, flow will become more 
southerly Friday, and southwesterly Saturday, shifting the sea 
breeze collision and highest chances for afternoon showers and 
lightning storms gradually farther into East Central Florida. Some
drier air will begin to intrude in the mid-upper levels, 
decreasing cloud cover some and offering better destabilization 
from daytime heating, and could also enhance downdrafts, 
potentially resulting in more storms capable of stronger gusts 
than previous days. A limiting factor for instability will be mid-
level temperatures which remain warm, and mostly occasional to 
frequent lightning is expected with storms. The main threat from 
storms will continue to be locally heavy rainfall of 2-4" and 
minor flooding from slow moving storms. There is a very low (up to
5%) chance for isolated spots to receive around 4" of rainfall 
leading to greater flooding impacts, and the Weather Prediction 
Center has outlooked all of East Central Florida in a Marginal 
(level 1 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall Friday, and will 
continue to monitor trends for Saturday. Temperatures creep up a 
degree or two as the onshore flow give ways to southerly and more 
sunlight peaks through the clouds, though we'll remain seasonably
hot with highs generally in the U80s-L90s, creeping towards the 
M90s inland. Muggy lows stay in the 70s.

Sunday-Wednesday...The trough over the eastern seaboard and
western Atlantic is forecast to reach just offshore the Southeast
seaboard Sunday or so, ushering a weakening front into the Deep
South, and possibly reaching Florida Monday or Tuesday. There
remains some uncertainty how far south the boundary will make it,
and more uncertainty where weak disturbances may develop on the
boundary as it stalls. Both impact whether East Central Florida
remains in the subtropical soup or if some drier air will finally
reach the area, what kinda of support there is for convection, and
what flow regime we end up in. Given the uncertainty the official
forecast trends towards the ensembles and blends, which call for
broad stroked rain chances to remain above normal, but do decrease
a bit towards mid-next week. Seasonable temperatures stay on the
